The study, carried out between October 2025 and January 2026, enrolled 1,132 participants using consecutive sampling to examine the prevalence and determinants of infection. Overall, the researchers detected an HPV prevalence of 33.6 percent, noting virtually identical burdens among younger and older demographics. Specifically, women aged 40 years and younger exhibited an infection rate of 33.6 percent, whereas participants aged 41 years and older had an infection rate of 33.4 percent. To obtain these clinical measurements, healthcare teams collected exfoliated cervical specimens from the participants and screened for high-risk HPV genotypes using the Hologic Panther platform paired with transcription-mediated amplification (TMA). In parallel, investigators administered structured questionnaires to capture detailed sociodemographic, behavioural, and reproductive information from each woman. To account for potential clustering of outcomes across different health facilities in the province, the analytical team applied mixed-effects logistic regression models to identify factors independently associated with viral infection. The statistical analyses revealed that the independent determinants of HPV infection diverged significantly depending on participant age. Among women aged 40 years and younger, infection was independently associated with a higher number of lifetime sexual partners, high parity, lack of HPV vaccination, contraceptive use, low income, single marital status, and attendance at rural healthcare facilities (P < 0.05). In contrast, among women aged 41 years and older, the independent risk factors comprised high parity, low HPV knowledge, unemployment, low income, and broader geographic location (P < 0.05). Beyond age-stratified predictors, the research group documented spatial variations in infection frequency across the study region, observing significantly elevated HPV rates within Mwandi district. The investigators noted that Zambia continues to experience one of the highest cervical cancer burdens globally, where human papillomavirus persists as a leading cause of cervical malignancy in low- and middle-income settings. In interpreting these patterns, the authors indicated that the substantial regional burden of HIV and ongoing transmission dynamics may also play a role in sustaining high levels of HPV infection across age groups. Reflecting on these contrasting associations, the study authors emphasize that interventions should be tailored to address the unique drivers identified within each age demographic. Rather than applying a uniform approach, the findings support integrated, age-specific prevention initiatives that combine HPV vaccination, routine cervical cancer screening, health education, and clinical treatment services to effectively curb the burden of HPV infection and its long-term health consequences across Western Province. Longitudinal surveillance over the five-year evaluation period revealed fluctuations in annual detection, with the infection rate rising from 15.30 percent in 2021 to a peak of 21.18 percent in 2023, before adjusting to 19.84 percent by 2025. Evaluation of viral infection patterns indicated that single infections predominated across the positive cohort, accounting for 75.83 percent of cases with 7,080 infected women displaying a single viral genotype. Analysis of age-stratified positivity demonstrated a bimodal distribution across demographic groups, reaching a first peak of 23.56 percent (810 of 3,438) among women aged 25 years or younger and a second peak of 26.05 percent (1,017 of 3,904) among women aged 56 years or older. Genotyping identified HPV52 as the most frequent variant with a prevalence of 3.62 percent (1,822 of 50,279), followed by HPV16 at 3.01 percent (1,514 of 50,279), HPV58 at 2.46 percent (1,239 of 50,279), HPV53 at 1.97 percent (989 of 50,279), and HPV39 at 1.72 percent (864 of 50,279), while HPV81 represented the most prevalent low-risk genotype at 1.70 percent (856 of 50,279). Annual genotype tracking showed that HPV53 prevalence increased significantly from 1.51 percent in 2021 to 2.72 percent in 2025 (P < 0.001), providing the largest localized epidemiological dataset to date to guide regional cervical cancer prevention and control strategies in Lianyungang. The clinical objective of the investigation centered on analyzing both the prevalence and genotype distribution of human papillomavirus infection across the population of Lianyungang, located in Northern Jiangsu Province, China. By systematically characterizing these viral patterns, the research was designed to provide localized epidemiological data necessary to support the prevention and treatment of cervical cancer and related diseases throughout the municipality. To evaluate these dynamics, the study design relied on a retrospective analysis of HPV genotyping records collected from 50,279 women at Lianyungang Maternal and Child Health Hospital between 2021 and 2025. The methodological evaluation systematically examined four distinct epidemiological parameters across the five-year surveillance period: overall infection rates, viral genotype distribution, age-specific positivity across demographic cohorts, and multi-year longitudinal trends. The research team concluded that the investigation provides the largest-scale dataset compiled to date regarding recent human papillomavirus epidemiology in Lianyungang. The authors noted that these localized empirical findings are intended to guide public health authorities in the development and implementation of regional cervical cancer prevention and disease control strategies. In evaluating the composition of positive cases, the researchers observed that solitary viral detection predominated over concurrent strains. The age-stratified data demonstrated that infection risk was concentrated at opposite extremes of the tested demographic spectrum. Women aged 56 years and older recorded the highest positivity rate across all evaluated groups at 26.05 percent (1,017 of 3,904), exceeding the initial peak of 23.56 percent (810 of 3,438) identified among women aged 25 years or younger. Regarding viral heterogeneity across the full sample of 50,279 women, the genotype hierarchy revealed distinct frequencies among dominant variants. HPV52 emerged as the most prevalent genotype at 3.62 percent (1,822 cases), followed by HPV16 at 3.01 percent (1,514 cases) and HPV58 at 2.46 percent (1,239 cases). HPV53 and HPV39 accounted for 1.97 percent (989 cases) and 1.72 percent (864 cases), respectively. In addition to these leading variants, the evaluation specifically classified HPV81 as the most common low-risk human papillomavirus genotype, affecting 1.70 percent of women (856 cases). content: 新闻 体育 汽车 房产 旅游 教育 时尚 科技 财经 娱乐 18岁少女检出18种HPV,高危型占10种! 2026-11-11 17:33 来源: 知识璞玉 当体检报告上赫然列出‘18种HPV亚型阳性’——其中10种是公认的‘致癌黑手’——连经验丰富的妇科医生都停顿了两秒。这不是科幻片桥段,而是发生在杭州临平区妇幼保健院的真实病例:一位18岁的女孩玲玲,因外阴持续疼痛半月就诊,最终被确诊为外阴尖锐湿疣,同时携带18种人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)亚型,高危型占比高达56%。 HPV不是‘一种病毒’,而是一支‘百变军团’ 很多人误以为HPV是单一病毒,实则它是一个拥有200多个已知亚型的庞大家族。按致癌风险,分为‘低危型’(如6、11型,主要引发尖锐湿疣)和‘高危型’(如16、18、33、45、52、58等,与宫颈癌、阴道癌、肛门癌密切相关)。全球约70%的宫颈癌由HPV16/18型导致,而我国年轻女性中,52、58型感染率甚至超过16型——这正是分型检测不可替代的关键所在。 一次检出18种?不是检测误差,而是免疫防线的‘失守警报’ 临床中,单次检出3–5种HPV亚型已属常见;检出10种以上即提示长期、反复、多途径暴露。玲玲的案例之所以罕见,并非因为‘病毒特别凶猛’,而在于她体内免疫系统未能及时识别并清除——就像一座城市同时遭遇18支不同番号的渗透小队,却迟迟未拉响防空警报。高病毒载量+多亚型共存,恰恰说明感染时间长、局部微环境紊乱、黏膜屏障功能受损,远期发展为CIN2+(高级别宫颈上皮内瘤变)的风险显著升高。 年轻≠安全,但也不等于‘判了死刑’ 值得强调的是:HPV感染不等于宫颈癌,更不等于‘必须切子宫’。数据显示,90%以上的年轻女性在1–2年内可凭借自身免疫力自然清除HPV,尤其在25岁以下群体中,清除率超95%。真正需要警惕的,是‘持续感染’——即同一高危型别在12个月内两次及以上阳性。玲玲的挑战在于‘多重叠加+高危主导’,因此治疗策略必须双线并进:物理祛除可见疣体(如激光/冷冻),同步启动免疫调节(营养干预+生活方式重建),而非盲目使用抗病毒药或过度手术。 给年轻女性的三条硬核建议 第一,别把HPV当成‘性污名标签’——它像感冒病毒一样普遍,一生中约80%的人会感染至少一次;第二,TCT(液基细胞学)和HPV分型必须联合做,单查HPV如同只看‘通缉令’不查‘现场证据’;第三,真正的‘疫苗’不在针管里,而在你的作息表上:睡眠不足4小时,NK细胞活性下降40%;吸烟者HPV清除时间延长3倍;BMI>28者,高危型持续感染风险翻倍。 玲玲正在接受规范治疗,也开启了人生第一次系统性健康管理。她的故事不是恐吓手册,而是一面镜子——照见我们对病毒的误解,也映出身体本就拥有的惊人自愈力。毕竟,最强大的宫颈癌防线,从来不在诊室,而在你规律的晚餐、充足的睡眠,和敢于说‘不’的边界感里。返回搜狐,查看更多 阅读 () 作者声明 含AI生成内容 平台声明 该文观点仅代表作者本人,搜狐号系信息发布平台,搜狐仅提供信息存储空间服务。

content: メインコンテンツへスキップ Questions to the Diet, Government Answers: What criteria will the government use to decide on routine HPV vaccination for males? Refundable やまと新聞 Nov 9, 2026 18:52 Basic Information Submitting Member: Koichi Mukoyama, Member of the House of Representatives (elected from the Kinki Proportional Representation Block, Parliamentary Group: Democratic Party for the People/Independent Club) Affiliated House: House of Representatives Diet Session: 222nd Diet Session (Extraordinary Session) Question Number: Question No. 10 Question Subject: Written Question Regarding Cost-Effectiveness Analysis for the Routine Vaccination of Males with the HPV Vaccine Submission Date: October 9, 2026 (Reiwa 8) Date Forwarded to Cabinet: October 19, 2026 Date of Answer (Date of Receipt of Written Answer): October 23, 2026 (Cabinet House Question No. 222-10) Introduction: Why is HPV vaccination for males a subject of debate? Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is known as the virus that causes cervical cancer. A supplementary fact sheet from the National Institute of Infectious Diseases (March 2024) states that HPV is also known to cause anal cancer, oropharyngeal cancer, and penile cancer, in addition to cervical cancer. Condyloma acuminatum, a type of benign wart, is also caused by HPV infection. However, not all of these cancers are caused by HPV. On the other hand, which diseases are recognized as being prevented by the vaccine is a separate issue. According to materials from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's council, the vaccines approved for use in males in Japan are the 4-valent vaccine (2020) and the 9-valent vaccine (August 2025), and the approved indications are for condyloma acuminatum and anal cancer (including its precursor lesions). The prevention of oropharyngeal cancer or penile cancer in males, and the prevention of cervical cancer in females through male vaccination, are not included in the pharmaceutical approvals. Since 2022, the government's council has been deliberating whether to include male vaccination in the 'routine vaccination' program funded by public expenses, but it has not yet reached the stage of routine vaccination. This question addresses the 'cost-effectiveness analysis' presented at the 35th meeting of the council's subcommittee (the Subcommittee on Vaccine Evaluation of the Health Sciences Council's Committee on Immunization and Vaccines, hereinafter 'the Subcommittee') held on July 22 of this year. Cost-effectiveness analysis is a method of numerically evaluating whether the health benefits of a vaccine justify its costs. What kind of lawmaker is the questioner? According to the official House of Representatives member information (as of April 2026), Koichi Mukoyama was born in Itami City, Hyogo Prefecture, in 1957. After graduating from the Faculty of Economics at Osaka University, he worked as an employee of Osaka Gas Co., Ltd., and as a public secretary to a member of the House of Representatives. He served two terms as a Kobe City Council member and two terms as a Hyogo Prefectural Assembly member. As a member of the House of Representatives, he has been elected three times and represents the Kinki Proportional Representation Block. He serves as the representative of the Democratic Party for the People's Hyogo Prefectural Federation and as a director of the House of Representatives Committee on the Environment. As for related past activities, Representative Mukoyama also submitted a 'Written Question Regarding the Early Routine Vaccination of Males with the HPV Vaccine' (Question No. 29) on July 2, 2026, during the previous Diet session (221st Diet Session). In a written answer dated July 14 of the same year, the government stated that it was striving to collect information regarding the effectiveness of routine vaccination. Regarding the motivation for this question, the editorial department could not confirm any materials in which the lawmaker himself explains it on his website or through statements in the Diet. content: No Result View All Result Scientists Develop Bean-Based Chewing Gum That Traps HPV in 93% of Tested Saliva Samples Share Share this article Facebook X LinkedIn Reddit WhatsApp Flipboard Bluesky Email Copy Link Comments Home → Health Scientists Develop Bean-Based Chewing Gum That Traps HPV in 93% of Tested Saliva Samples It traps HPV and kills cancer-associated bacteria. But can it prevent cancer? byTudor Tarita November 13, 2026 in Diseases, Future, Health, News A A A A Reset Edited and reviewed by Mihai Andrei Loading Audio Player By Instaread, Please Wait... Not the actual gum. Credit: Wikimedia Commons A potential new weapon against cancer-linked infections comes in mint flavor; and its secret ingredient comes from an unlikely place: beans. Scientists have developed a chewing gum that might one day help fight cancer-linked infections. And in laboratory tests involving saliva from cancer patients, the results were surprisingly promising. Bean Protein vs. Cancer-Causing Virus HPV is one of the world’s most common sexually transmitted infections. Most infections disappear naturally, but some persist for years. Certain strains can eventually cause cancer, and in the mouth, HPV can create tumors around the tonsils and at the base of the tongue. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, HPV causes an estimated 60% to 70% of cancers in the back of the throat in the United States. Researchers led by Henry Daniell, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine, wondered whether they could capture HPV particles in the mouth before they infect additional cells or spread to another person. Their solution involved the lablab bean, also called the hyacinth bean. It naturally contains an antiviral protein called FRIL, which binds to sugars on the surfaces of viruses. Lablab purpureus and the resulting gum. Credit: Scientific Reports (2026) Imagine throwing a sticky net over a swarm of insects. This FRIL protein works somewhat similarly, linking virus particles into large clumps that can potentially prevent them from entering human cells. The researchers incorporated this protein into an experimental chewing gum. They then tested extracts from it against HPV in saliva and mouth-rinse samples collected from patients with head and neck cancer. × Get smarter every day... Stay ahead with ZME Science and subscribe. Sign Up Free Daily Newsletter The science you need to know, every weekday. Weekly Newsletter A week in science, all in one place. Sends every Sunday. No spam, ever. Unsubscribe anytime. Review our Privacy Policy. Thank you! One more thing... Please check your inbox and confirm your subscription. After mixing the extracts with the samples, they separated out the viral clumps and measured how much HPV remained in the liquid. The results were striking. HPV particles aggregated in 13 of 14 saliva samples. The extent varied, but several samples showed reductions of more than 85% in detectable HPV after treatment. In HPV-positive mouth-rinse samples, the researchers reported an approximately 80% reduction in the viral signal. In total, the HPV experiments drew on samples from 44 cancer patients. Illustration of how FRIL traps HPV. Credit: Scientific Reports (2026) But why chewing gum rather than a pill? “Oral medicines get diluted in blood and are not suitable for concentrated local delivery at the site of infection,” Daniell told Women’s Health. Chewing gum could release antiviral proteins precisely where they’re needed, rather than distributing them throughout the body. There’s another advantage: the protein comes from a plant that can be cultivated relatively cheaply. And researchers have already developed gum tablets containing the ingredient, rather than merely proposing the idea on paper. A Second Ingredient Goes After Bacteria HPV wasn’t the researchers’ only target. Two bacterial species, Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum, have also been associated with poorer outcomes in some patients with head and neck cancer. They can promote inflammation and interfere with the body’s defenses, although their precise role in cancer isn’t entirely clear. Fusobacterium. Credit: Wikimedia Commons. The researchers combined the bean gum extract with protegrin-1, an antimicrobial peptide that damages bacterial membranes. The combination proved remarkably potent. After one hour of treatment, it reduced both targeted bacterial species by more than 99% in laboratory-tested patient samples. Interestingly, the treatment appeared to spare some of the mouth’s normal bacterial residents. Certain streptococci, which are commonly found in a healthy oral microbiome, proved more resistant, possibly because protective capsules shield them from the antimicrobial compound. This raises the intriguing possibility of targeting harmful bacteria without wiping out their beneficial neighbors. However, this needs to be investigated in closer detail, the researchers suggest.. Eliminating harmful species without extensively disturbing beneficial ones could be especially valuable for cancer patients, whose treatments sometimes disrupt their oral microbiome. The approach also builds on earlier research from Daniell’s team, which found that bean-derived antiviral chewing gum could neutralize influenza and herpes viruses in laboratory experiments. Could Chewing Gum Actually Prevent Cancer? Credit: Pexels, As encouraging as this is, it’s important to take a step back and look at the big picture. There’s an enormous difference between trapping HPV in a laboratory sample and preventing cancer in a living person. The researchers measured viral aggregation, not whether the gum stopped infections, prevented transmission, or reduced tumor growth. They also don’t know how long any protective effect would last inside the mouth. RelatedPosts This bacterium shoots wires out of its body to power itself Synthetic jellyfish made from rat heart cells can swim like the real deal In Denmark, a Vaccine Is Eliminating a Type of Cervical Cancer Therapeutic vaccine shows promise of treatment against HPV infections that lead to cancer Paolo Serafini, an immunologist at the University of Miami who wasn’t involved in the research, raised precisely this concern. “We do not know how long the gum can take the bacteria and virus away,” Serafini told Women’s Health. “My guess is for an hour. That is not going to have a big impact.” There’s also the question of what happens after the effect wears off. Would pathogens rapidly return? Would people have to chew several pieces every day? And could repeated exposure disturb the delicate balance of microbes that normally inhabit the mouth? And trapping viruses in saliva doesn’t necessarily eliminate infections already established in the tissues of the mouth and throat. A lablab pod. Image via Wiki Commons. HPV vaccination remains the established preventive measure against cancer-causing HPV types. The experimental gum would not replace vaccination, cancer screening, or conventional treatments. Still, Daniell believes the technology deserves clinical testing. In an August interview with the New York Post, he described plans for a four-week trial in which participants would chew the gum three times daily, pending regulatory approval. He also argued that plant-derived proteins could make the treatment unusually inexpensive to manufacture. If human trials confirm that the gum works safely and consistently inside the mouth, it could eventually offer a convenient way to reduce exposure to certain cancer-linked microbes. For now, it’s an inventive laboratory experiment, not a cancer treatment. But the idea is compelling: instead of waiting for a dangerous infection to do damage, perhaps one day we could chew away at the risk. The study was published in the journal Scientific Reports. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 14, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Cameroon Evaluates Cervical Cancer Strategy Progress and Health System Hurdles in Scale-Up by November 12, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Cameroon Evaluates Cervical Cancer Strategy Progress and Health System Hurdles in Scale-Up Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A structured narrative synthesis published in Frontiers in Medicine has evaluated Cameroon’s operational progress toward implementing the World Health Organization global strategy for cervical cancer elimination, highlighting substantial advances in prevention alongside critical health-system bottlenecks. Synthesizing peer-reviewed publications and official technical documents released between 2015 and 2026, the review examines how Cameroon has introduced innovative primary and secondary prevention initiatives to combat a disease that remains one of the most frequently diagnosed malignancies among Cameroonian women. Although the World Health Organization established ambitious 90-70-90 targets to be reached by 2030—calling for 90 percent of girls to be fully vaccinated against human papillomavirus by age 15, 70 percent of women to undergo high-performance screening at ages 35 and 45, and 90 percent of diagnosed women to receive treatment—the synthesis reveals that national coverage indicators remain substantially below these elimination thresholds. The biological rationale underpinning these prevention efforts stems from persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus genotypes, which serves as the established necessary cause for the development of invasive cervical carcinoma and its precursor lesions. Within low- and middle-income countries, where more than 90 percent of global cervical cancer deaths occur, structural inequities in healthcare access exacerbate disease progression and mortality. In Cameroon, the intersection between human papillomavirus and human immunodeficiency virus represents a profound public health concern, as women living with human immunodeficiency virus experience impaired immune clearance that drives significantly elevated rates of viral persistence, rapid advancement to high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, and an increased incidence of invasive cancer. Consequently, international guidelines recommend initiating screening at earlier ages and maintaining shorter recall intervals for this priority population. The review underscores that addressing these clinical risks requires robust primary prevention via prophylactic immunization alongside sensitive secondary screening algorithms that detect cellular and molecular abnormalities long before malignant transformation occurs. Discover more cancers health Get Health Tips National primary prevention in Cameroon commenced formally in October 2020 with the introduction of human papillomavirus vaccination into the routine immunization schedule, though early uptake was hindered by logistical and social obstacles. Programmatic progress improved noticeably following the strategic adoption of a gender-neutral, single-dose vaccination policy coupled with intensified community-level distribution mechanisms. By 2023, national coverage reached approximately 57 percent among eligible girls and approximately 26 percent among boys, marking notable progress while remaining well below the 90 percent World Health Organization elimination benchmark. Structural delivery challenges persist, including difficulties in identifying and vaccinating out-of-school adolescent populations, recurring distribution disruptions across medical supply chains, and the limited integration of immunization campaigns into routine adolescent healthcare platforms. Furthermore, sociobehavioral barriers such as circulating misinformation, low perceived personal risk, and general vaccine hesitancy continue to depress community demand. Overcoming these deficits requires coordinated intersectoral collaboration among the Ministries of Health, Education, and Finance, reinforced by comprehensive electronic vaccination registries that can monitor equity gaps and guide adaptive local outreach. Discover more Find Cancer Care See an OB-GYN Cancer cancer The Cameroon Baptist Convention Health Services Women's Health Program is the largest cervical cancer screening initiative in the country and provides an important service-delivery platform in the absence of nationwide programme expansion. More recently, decentralized implementation pilots conducted in Dschang, Bafoussam, and Yaoundé demonstrated the feasibility of simplified screen-triage-treat protocols, commonly designated as the Test-Triage-Treat approach. Decentralization should be considered a core component of national scale-up, using the tiered service-delivery infrastructure already being developed for HIV testing and treatment in Cameroon. Peripheral level-one health centers and intermediate level-two district facilities could be equipped to perform point-of-care human papillomavirus nucleic acid testing and visual inspection triage, while complex cytopathology remains anchored at specialized regional laboratories possessing appropriate technical personnel. Task-shifting represents an essential component of this structural reorganization, transferring routine primary testing, self-sampling guidance, visual triage, and local thermal ablation procedures to trained nurses and certified midwives. The authors stress that delegating these clinical responsibilities requires institutionalizing standardized clinical protocols, formal competency-based instructional curricula, regular supportive supervision, and robust quality-assurance mechanisms. Without standardized tracking mechanisms and continuous oversight, decentralized screening risks generating inconsistent diagnostic assessments or failing to route complex lesions into appropriate tertiary surgical channels, thereby blunting the epidemiological impact of expanded community-level screening. Integrating cervical screening into routine clinical care for women living with human immunodeficiency virus constitutes another vital strategic opportunity to optimize resource utilization and elevate healthcare equity. Because differentiated service-delivery models are well established in HIV care in Cameroon, projects such as OptiTri are exploring how these platforms can be extended to incorporate cervical cancer screening. In these models, human papillomavirus testing, including self-sampling, can be integrated into routine antiretroviral therapy services, with triage and treatment organized as close as possible to the point of screening. Emerging programme experience suggests that co-location of cervical cancer screening within HIV services can improve uptake, shorten the interval between testing, diagnosis, and treatment, and reduce attrition across the screening cascade. However, scaling this integrated model nationwide demands uninterrupted reagent procurement, clearly delineated clinical handoffs between infectious disease personnel and gynecological specialists, and rigorous tracking of programmatic performance indicators, including screening uptake rates, viral genotype positivity, and long-term retention within routine post-treatment surveillance. Advancements in molecular diagnostics have introduced sophisticated risk-stratified triage algorithms that balance analytical sensitivity against the clinical hazard of unnecessary surgical intervention. While standard human papillomavirus testing is highly sensitive for cervical precancer, it often detects transient infections that would resolve spontaneously without clinical consequence. Extended genotyping enables clinicians to tailor secondary management according to the distinct oncogenic hazard posed by specific viral variants. The recent World Health Organization classification delineates twelve carcinogenic human papillomavirus genotypes into four distinct risk strata: group 1a consisting exclusively of type 16; group 1b containing types 18 and 45; group 1c comprising types 31, 33, 35, 52, and 58; and group 1d encompassing types 39, 51, 56, and 59. Evidence from Cameroon indicates that resource-adapted algorithms can route women positive for type 16 directly to ablative treatment, while directing those carrying intermediate-risk genotypes to visual or telecytological triage, reserving conservative observational surveillance for lower-risk variants. When extended genotyping of all twelve carcinogenic human papillomavirus types is not feasible, a simplified eight-genotype panel covering groups 1a through 1c may simplify testing while retaining coverage of the types responsible for the largest proportion of cervical cancers. Complementing molecular triage, digital telemedicine innovations and artificial intelligence applications are being evaluated across Cameroon to bridge severe shortages of specialized medical personnel. Telecytology platforms utilizing whole-slide digital imaging allow remote cytopathologists to examine digitized cervical smears collected at peripheral and district facilities, demonstrating high diagnostic concordance with conventional microscopy while decentralizing specialist expertise. In parallel, investigational computer-aided diagnostic algorithms designed to interpret cervical photographs following acetic acid application and automated digital cytology are being explored to mitigate the known operator subjectivity of visual inspection. Nevertheless, the review urges measured caution, noting that existing artificial intelligence evaluations in Cameroon rely predominantly on small, highly curated image datasets that do not reflect routine screening populations encountered in frontline clinics. The authors assert that artificial intelligence tools remain strictly experimental and must undergo rigorous prospective clinical validation, external verification, cost-effectiveness analyses, and formal regulatory oversight before being integrated into routine national clinical practice. For patients diagnosed with invasive cervical carcinoma, the national healthcare infrastructure exhibits severe diagnostic and therapeutic deficiencies that compromise curative intent. Effective oncological care requires standardized national staging guidelines supported by reliable histopathology, specialized surgical oncology teams, multimodal chemoradiotherapy, and decentralized palliative care. The therapeutic deficit is especially acute for locally advanced tumors requiring definitive radiation therapy, as functional megavoltage external-beam radiotherapy equipment nationwide remains concentrated exclusively in Douala, creating a severe geographical bottleneck. Furthermore, because a high proportion of Cameroonian cervical cancer patients present with incurable advanced-stage malignancy, palliative care represents an essential clinical requirement; however, palliative services remain largely fragmented, heavily reliant on faith-based charitable organizations, and constrained by restricted community access to oral opioid analgesics. Sustaining national scale-up ultimately requires establishing robust institutional governance, sustainable health financing, and resilient digital monitoring systems capable of tracking patients across fragmented health jurisdictions. Digital health platforms must provide offline operational functionality to withstand intermittent electrical and internet connectivity, while remaining fully interoperable with national health management databases such as the District Health Information Software 2 platform. Automated text-messaging appointment reminders and digital notification systems can significantly reduce diagnostic loss to follow-up and enhance clinical recall. Methodologically, the authors emphasize that their synthesis represents a narrative review of heterogeneous programmatic reports, observational pilots, and technical documents rather than a systematic meta-analysis, noting that empirical gaps persist regarding longitudinal health outcomes, formal cost-effectiveness, and equitable community uptake. Ultimately, eliminating cervical cancer in Cameroon will depend not on isolated technical innovations, but on sustained political leadership, coordinated domestic financing, structured implementation research, and patient-centered service delivery that respects community trust and addresses the real-world operational constraints of resource-limited healthcare environments. Science News from research organizations Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93% Date: November 10, 2026 Source: University of Pennsylvania Summary: A surprising new weapon against microbes linked to head and neck cancer could be as simple as chewing gum. Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract. Even more promising, the treatment spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth. Share: Facebook Twitter Pinterest LinkedIN Email FULL STORY A specially engineered chewing gum could become an unexpected weapon against head and neck cancer by targeting harmful viruses and bacteria while leaving beneficial microbes unharmed. Credit: Shutterstock A specially engineered chewing gum could offer an unexpected new weapon against viruses and bacteria linked to head and neck cancer. In laboratory tests using samples from cancer patients, researchers found that extracts from the gum reduced levels of human papillomavirus, or HPV, by as much as 93%. An enhanced version also nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species while leaving beneficial bacteria unharmed. The findings, reported in Scientific Reports, suggest that this experimental approach could eventually help prevent certain infections and support existing cancer treatments. Researchers believe the plant-based technology could also provide a more affordable option for patients. The research was led by Henry Daniell of the University of Pennsylvania's School of Dental Medicine. His team has been exploring ways to use specially engineered plants to produce proteins with potential medical benefits. Why Scientists Are Targeting Cancer-Linked Microbes Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a common form of cancer that develops in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. It begins in squamous cells, the thin, flat cells that cover many surfaces throughout the body. These cancers can be particularly difficult to treat once they have spread, and patients diagnosed at advanced stages often face poor outcomes. According to Daniell, recently approved cancer medications have generally failed to produce major improvements in patients' quality of life or their chances of surviving five years after diagnosis. This highlights the continuing need for more effective treatments and new strategies that could help prevent the disease or reduce complications. One promising area of research involves the microorganisms living in the mouth. Although many oral microbes are harmless or beneficial, certain viruses and bacteria have been associated with the development or progression of head and neck cancers. The researchers focused on three of these microbes. The first was HPV, a common virus that can cause certain cancers when infections persist. The other two were Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn), bacterial species associated with oral disease and poorer outcomes in some cancer patients. "The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection," says Daniell. "And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies." Oropharyngeal cancer affects the middle portion of the throat, including areas such as the tonsils and base of the tongue. Metastatic cancer refers to cancer that has spread beyond its original location, while adjuvant treatments are additional therapies given to improve the effectiveness of primary treatment. A Chewing Gum Made From Beans Delivers Surprising Results The new study builds on the team's earlier development of a chewing gum made from lablab beans (bean gum). This gum contains FRIL, a naturally occurring protein with antiviral properties. To investigate its potential benefits, the scientists tested extracts from the gum against microbes found in oral samples collected from patients with head and neck cancer. The results were striking. The bean gum extracts lowered HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples and by 80% in oral rinse samples. These findings suggest that proteins delivered through a chewing gum could potentially help reduce the presence of a virus associated with certain head and neck cancers. The team then took the technology a step further by engineering the gum to contain protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Some antimicrobial peptides can attack and destroy harmful microorganisms, making them promising candidates for new infection treatments. With this additional ingredient, the researchers found that a single dose of the engineered gum extract reduced the two targeted bacterial species, Pg and Fn, to almost undetectable levels. Harmful Bacteria Nearly Disappear While Good Bacteria Survive One of the most encouraging findings was the gum's ability to target harmful bacteria without disrupting the beneficial microorganisms that naturally inhabit the mouth. The oral microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microscopic organisms living inside the mouth, plays an important role in maintaining oral health. Many of these microbes coexist harmlessly with the body and help maintain a balanced environment. Some cancer treatments can disturb that balance. Radiation therapy, for example, can reduce populations of beneficial oral bacteria while encouraging the growth of potentially harmful yeast, including Candida albicans. In contrast, the experimental gum extract sharply reduced the targeted bacteria without affecting the beneficial bacterial populations examined by the researchers. This selectivity could be especially valuable for patients whose oral health has already been affected by cancer or its treatment. Importantly, the results came from laboratory testing of patient samples rather than clinical trials in which people chewed the gum. Further research will be needed to determine whether the same effects occur in the human mouth and whether reducing these microbes can meaningfully improve cancer outcomes. Could Chewing Gum Become Part of Cancer Prevention and Treatment? The researchers believe their findings justify moving the technology toward human clinical trials, particularly because head and neck cancers remain a serious global health challenge. "Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022," says Daniell. "Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission." Prophylaxis refers to measures taken to prevent disease or infection before it occurs. In this case, the researchers envision a future in which specially designed chewing gum might help limit exposure to harmful microbes or reduce their levels in people already receiving cancer treatment. Such an approach could offer a relatively simple and potentially inexpensive way to deliver protective proteins directly into the mouth, where the targeted microorganisms are found. For now, the technology remains experimental, and there is no evidence yet that chewing the gum prevents or treats cancer in humans. Nevertheless, the ability to substantially reduce HPV and nearly eliminate two cancer-associated bacterial species in laboratory tests offers a promising starting point for further investigation. If future clinical trials confirm its safety and effectiveness, a familiar everyday product could become an unexpected addition to the medical toolkit against dangerous oral infections and cancers. 【大纪元2026年11月12日讯】浙江省杭州市一名年仅18岁的女子,被确诊外阴尖锐湿疣,一次检出18种人类乳头瘤病毒(HPV)亚型阳性,其中10种属于高危型。这宗罕见的多重感染病例近日引起关注,相关话题“杭州18岁女孩检出18种HPV亚型阳性”登上微博热搜。 潮新闻等大陆媒体报导,近日,杭州市临平区妇幼保健院妇科接诊了一例极其少见的HPV多重感染病例:年仅18岁的玲玲因外阴持续性疼痛半月余前来就诊,最终确诊为外阴尖锐湿疣。 接诊医生检查发现,玲玲外阴长有菜花状赘生物,外观疑似尖锐湿疣。其后进行HPV分型检测,结果显示共有18种亚型阳性,其中高危型多达10种。最终诊断为外阴尖锐湿疣及HPV多重感染。医生判断其病毒暴露时间长、感染复杂,远期癌变风险显著升高。 院方表示,这类多亚型混合感染在临床上较为少见,尤其是同时检出多种高危型,患者需要接受规范治疗及长期随访。 尖锐湿疣由人乳头瘤病毒感染所致,多表现为生殖器部位菜花状赘生物,可伴随疼痛、异物感。世界卫生组织(WHO)指出,持续感染高危型HPV是宫颈癌的主要致病因素。从感染到发展为癌症通常需要较长时间,并非检测呈阳性便会立即癌变。透过适当筛查、追踪及治疗癌前病变,可以降低宫颈癌发生风险。 医生介绍,大多数生殖道HPV感染可依靠自身免疫力,1年至2年内自行清除病毒,属于一过性感染,不等于宫颈癌。高危型HPV持续感染才会导致宫颈癌前病变或宫颈癌的发生;单纯HPV阳性、TCT正常≠癌前病变。一般年轻女性HPV感染率高。 世界卫生组织建议,9至14岁女孩应优先接种HPV疫苗,以便在可能接触病毒前建立保护。美国疾病控制与预防中心(CDC)指出,即使已感染某一种HPV型别,接种疫苗仍可能预防其它尚未感染、且属于疫苗涵盖范围的型别;但HPV疫苗属于预防性疫苗,不能治疗已存在的感染。 责任编辑:方晓 标签 杭州女子18种HPV亚型阳性 如果您有新闻线索或资料给大纪元,请进入安全投稿爆料平台。 新闻排行 Show results from: Clear search input Search for result Max Clear search input Search for result Press release Cambodia accelerates cervical cancer prevention through HPV Multi-Age-Cohort Vaccination Campaign for adolescent girls 10 November 2026 UNICEF Cambodia/2026/Seavhong Liv English Khmer Phnom Penh, 10 November 2026 – The Royal Government of Cambodia, through the Ministry of Health and the National Immunization Programme (NIP), today launched a nationwide Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Multi-Age Cohort (MAC) vaccination campaign, which vaccinates multiple age groups of adolescent girls at the same time, and catch-up vaccination, expanding protection against cervical cancer for adolescent girls across the country. Cervical cancer remains a major public health challenge in Cambodia and is the second leading cancer among women of all agesi. Nearly all cervical cancer cases are linked to persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, making HPV vaccination one of the most effective preventive measuresii. Together with cervical cancer screening and early treatment of precancerous lesions, HPV vaccination forms the cornerstone of global efforts to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem. Building on the successful introduction of HPV vaccine into Cambodia’s National Immunization Programme in 2023, the campaign will be implemented alongside routine HPV vaccination for 9-year-old girls. It will provide free HPV vaccination to all girls aged 13–14 years, while offering catch-up vaccination for girls aged 10–12 years who may have missed vaccination through the routine programme in 2023–2025. This catch-up approach is intended to close remaining immunity gaps and ensure protection for girls who were not vaccinated when eligible. In line with WHO recommendations, a single dose of HPV vaccine provides strong and durable protection against HPV infection and cervical cancer. To maximize coverage, the nationwide campaign will be implemented in two phases from November to December 2026. The campaign reflects Cambodia's continued commitment to preventing cervical cancer and ensuring healthier futures for women and girls. Implementation is being coordinated in collaboration with the Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport (MoEYS), national and subnational government authorities, and community partners, with support from Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance (Gavi), the World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), and the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI). Launching the campaign, H.E. Professor Chheang Ra, Minister of Health, reaffirmed Cambodia's commitment to protecting future generations from cervical cancer. "Every girl deserves protection from cervical cancer. By expanding HPV vaccination opportunities across the country, we are ensuring that girls who missed previous opportunities can still benefit from this safe, effective and life-saving vaccine. We appeal to parents, caregivers, teachers, health workers and local authorities to work together so that every eligible girl can be reached and protected." The campaign will be delivered through coordinated school-based, community-based, and health facility-based vaccination approaches. Vaccination teams will work closely with teachers, Village Health Support Groups, local authorities and community leaders to identify and reach all eligible girls, with particular focus on those who are absent from school or living in hard-to-reach communities. “HPV vaccination is one of the most effective tools for preventing cervical cancer,” emphasized Dr Marianna Trias, WHO Representative to Cambodia. “WHO recommends vaccinating girls aged 9–14 years, before they are exposed to HPV. By expanding vaccination opportunities for girls up to age 14, Cambodia is accelerating progress towards eliminating cervical cancer while safeguarding the health and well-being of future generations.” The central objective of the campaign is to ensure that no eligible girl is left behind, especially girls who are out of school and living in remote and hard-to-reach communities. Community engagement, social mobilization, school participation and local leadership will play central roles in helping families understand the benefits and safety of HPV vaccination and know when and where vaccination services are available. "Every eligible girl should have access to HPV vaccination, regardless of where she lives or whether she attends school," said Ms. Maha Damaj, UNICEF Representative to Cambodia. “Reaching those most at risk of being left behind is essential to ensuring that protection against cervical cancer is available to all,” she added. The campaign also draws on lessons learned from previous HPV vaccination activities in Cambodia, particularly in identifying eligible girls, strengthening microplanning, improving community engagement and ensuring accurate monitoring throughout implementation. "Cambodia has already demonstrated strong leadership in introducing HPV vaccination," said Mr. Lan Mao, acting Director of CHAI Cambodia. "This campaign builds on that success by strengthening the systems needed to identify, reach and vaccinate all eligible girls, particularly those who may otherwise be missed." National HPV vaccination programmes are now established in more than 162 countries worldwide, protecting millions of lives. In low- and middle-income countries, Gavi-supported efforts have protected 95 million girls, preventing an estimated 1.9 million future deaths from cervical cancer. HPV vaccination is among the most impactful interventions Gavi supports, averting an estimated 13 deaths for every 1,000 children vaccinated. “We commend the Government for its outstanding partnership and its efforts to control cervical cancer through investments in screening, treatment, and prevention programmes. This campaign demonstrates what is possible when national leadership is matched by sustained investment,” said Priya Gajraj, Director, Core Countries at Gavi. “HPV vaccination is among the most impactful interventions Gavi supports. With more than USD 3 million in funding for this campaign, which aims to protect more than 700,000 girls in schools and communities, Gavi reaffirms our commitment to support Cambodia in its efforts to build stronger links between adolescent girls and essential health services.” The multi-age cohort campaign and catch-up vaccination, together with routine HPV vaccination, will help close immunity gaps, increase protection against HPV infection, and contribute to Cambodia's long-term goal of eliminating cervical cancer as a public health problem throughout the country. Notes to editors: Gavi supports lower-income countries to introduce and sustain national HPV vaccination programmes by financing vaccines, delivery and campaigns, strengthening immunization systems and technical assistance, and helping shape a more secure and affordable global vaccine market. By the end of 2025, Gavi had supported 53 countries to launch national HPV programmes, fully immunizing more than 95 million girls and helping avert an estimated 1.9 million future cervical cancer deaths. Through its wider HPV programme, Gavi is working with countries and partners to expand equitable coverage, reach girls missed by school-based services and integrate vaccination into broader adolescent health efforts. The Vaccine Alliance brings together developing country and donor governments, the World Health Organization, UNICEF, the World Bank, the vaccine industry, technical agencies, civil society, the Gates Foundation and other private sector partners. View the full list of donor governments and other leading organizations that fund Gavi’s work here. Since its inception in 2000, Gavi has helped to immunize a whole generation – over 1.3 billion children – and prevented more than 23 million future deaths, helping to halve child mortality in 78 lower‐income countries. Gavi also plays a key role in improving global health security by supporting health systems as well as funding global stockpiles for Ebola, cholera, meningococcal, mpox and yellow fever vaccines. After more than two decades of progress, Gavi is now focused on protecting the next generation, above all the zero-dose children who have not received even a single vaccine shot. The Vaccine Alliance employs innovative finance and the latest technology – from drones to biometrics – to save lives, prevent outbreaks before they can spread and help countries on the road to self-sufficiency. These efforts aim to improve access to quality healthcare, promote health equity, and ensure better health outcomes for all Cambodians, with particular attention to poor, vulnerable, and underserved communities. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 14, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Rapid Cervical Cancer Antigen Test Shows High Agreement With Standard DNA Assay by November 13, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Rapid Cervical Cancer Antigen Test Shows High Agreement With Standard DNA Assay Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A rapid point-of-care cervical screening test targeting viral oncoproteins demonstrated near-perfect diagnostic agreement with standard high-risk human papillomavirus deoxyribonucleic acid testing in a resource-limited setting, according to a cross-sectional study. Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus accounts for an estimated 97 to 99 percent of cervical cancer cases worldwide. Although molecular assays detecting viral deoxyribonucleic acid remain the reference standard for early detection, their implementation in low-resource environments is often restricted by high equipment costs and specialized technical requirements. To investigate a potentially accessible alternative, researchers evaluated the MobiLab rapid oncoprotein E6/E7 antigen test against polymerase chain reaction testing on the Cobas 4800 platform. The investigated antigen test targets the active expression of E6 and E7 oncoproteins, which are directly associated with malignant cellular transformation. Evaluating whether such rapid tests correspond accurately with validated deoxyribonucleic acid platforms is critical for understanding their utility in decentralized screening programs. The cross-sectional investigation took place between February and July 2024 at Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital. The study cohort comprised 257 randomly selected women aged 30 years and older who presented for routine cervical cancer screening. For each participant, healthcare providers collected a cervical swab designated for high-risk human papillomavirus testing using polymerase chain reaction, followed by an additional cervical sample obtained using a Delphi vaginal sampler for the MobiLab rapid antigen evaluation. Discover more Research report templates Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Donate to Research The Cobas 4800 platform served as the reference standard in the comparative analysis. As a qualitative, real-time polymerase chain reaction assay, the platform amplifies target sequences within the L1 region of the high-risk human papillomavirus genome. It identifies 14 distinct oncogenic viral types, providing specific detection for types 16 and 18, alongside 12 other high-risk types including 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66, and 68. Across the entire cohort, the MobiLab rapid oncoprotein test yielded an overall positivity rate of 58.0 percent, identifying positive results in 149 of the 257 participants. Cross-tabulation between the rapid antigen method and the Cobas 4800 molecular assay revealed concordant classifications in nearly all cases. Specifically, 148 of 149 positive results and 107 of 108 negative results were classified identically by both diagnostic platforms. Statistical evaluation demonstrated an overall diagnostic agreement of 99.22 percent between the two testing methods. The positive agreement rate reached 99.33 percent, while the negative agreement rate was calculated at 99.07 percent. Assessment of inter-assay concordance yielded a Cohen’s kappa coefficient of 0.992, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning from 0.96 to 1.00, achieving statistical significance with a two-tailed p-value below 0.001. Comparative performance metrics further confirmed high diagnostic fidelity relative to the molecular reference standard. The rapid antigen assay achieved a sensitivity of 99.33 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 96.32 to 99.98 percent, and a specificity of 99.07 percent, with a confidence interval of 94.95 to 99.98 percent. The calculated positive predictive value was 99.33 percent, while the negative predictive value was 99.07 percent, accompanied by an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.992. Discover more Find Conferences Find Study Aids Cancer research funding Get Health Tips Health The study authors concluded that findings from the MobiLab rapid oncoprotein E6/E7 antigen test closely match the results generated by the Cobas 4800 assay. However, they emphasized that further investigations incorporating definitive cytological, colposcopic, and histopathological endpoints are essential to fully establish clinical validity and define the role of this point-of-care tool within resource-constrained screening systems. The MobiLab rapid oncoprotein E6/E7 antigen test functions as a point-of-care alternative designed to identify active oncogene expression associated with malignant transformation. Unlike standard molecular assays that detect viral deoxyribonucleic acid, this antigen-based approach targets the specific proteins produced by the virus. The study authors noted that while molecular assays are considered the gold standard for screening and early detection, their widespread use in low-resource settings is often hindered by significant cost barriers and demanding technical requirements. The MobiLab test offers a potentially accessible option for decentralized screening programs where such infrastructure is limited. This design allowed researchers to compare the two testing methods simultaneously within the same cohort of participants. Participants were randomly selected from those undergoing routine screening at Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, ensuring a representative group for the comparative analysis. Statistical analysis included the calculation of Cohen’s kappa coefficient to assess inter-rater reliability between the two assays. The study also utilized receiver operating characteristic curves to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of the rapid test relative to the reference standard. The authors highlighted that the current findings do not yet establish the clinical validity of the MobiLab test for definitive diagnosis. They emphasized the need for further studies that incorporate cytological, colposcopic, and histopathological endpoints. These additional diagnostic steps are necessary to determine the test’s true role in screening programs. Without these endpoints, the agreement with DNA testing remains a measure of diagnostic concordance rather than a confirmation of clinical utility. content: 女孩查出18种HPV含10种高危致癌型 罕见多重感染病例引发关注 钱江晚报 2026-11-12 08:29:12 A+ A- 近日,杭州市临平区妇幼保健院妇科接诊了一例极其少见的HPV多重感染病例。18岁的玲玲因外阴持续性疼痛半月余前来就诊,最终确诊为外阴尖锐湿疣,并一次性检出18种HPV亚型阳性,其中高危型多达10种,属于临床极少见的多重混合感染。 玲玲来杭探亲期间,外阴隐隐疼痛,总觉得有异物感,最近症状愈发严重,影响了正常生活。专科查体发现其外阴长了典型的菜花状赘生物,外观类似尖锐湿疣。为了明确感染的具体病毒类型,医生给她做了高精度HPV分型检测,结果显示共18种HPV亚型同时阳性,且病毒载量很高。 在18种阳性亚型中,包含10种高危致癌型HPV,这些亚型是诱发宫颈上皮内病变甚至进展为宫颈癌的主要风险因素。一次性多重混合感染18种亚型且高危占比极高,提示患者病毒暴露时间长、感染复杂、远期癌变风险显著升高。结合玲玲的症状、专科体征及精准HPV分型结果,医生最终确诊她为外阴尖锐湿疣和HPV多重高危感染,目前正在进行积极治疗。 尖锐湿疣由人乳头瘤病毒感染引起,多表现为生殖器部位的菜花状赘生物,可伴随疼痛和异物感。该患者同时合并多亚型HPV混合感染,尤其是多种高危型持续感染,远期存在宫颈病变风险,需要规范治疗并长期随访复查。 对于年轻未生育女性感染HPV的情况,医生建议重点进行分层评估,避免过度治疗,以保护生育功能。大多数生殖道HPV感染依靠自身免疫力,在1至2年内自行清除病毒,属于一过性感染,并不等于宫颈癌。只有高危型HPV持续感染才会导致宫颈癌前病变或宫颈癌的发生;单纯HPV阳性、TCT正常并不等同于癌前病变。年轻女性虽然HPV感染率较高,但病毒清除能力强,因此不必过度恐慌。 提高自身免疫力是清除病毒的关键,建议规律睡眠、减重、均衡饮食,戒烟(吸烟会显著降低病毒清除率,增加病变进展风险),适度运动,避免长期熬夜和巨大精神压力。此外,性生活时建议全程佩戴避孕套,减少交叉反复感染的风险。(责任编辑:zx0176) 责任编辑:zx0176 点击查看全文(剩余84%) 热点新闻 南京零元面馆周围7家店转让 善举引发周边商铺经营困境 2026-11-14 07:18:32 湖北连夜开会就王忠林被查表态 反腐无死角 2026-11-14 00:06:17 一张地图 怎么就逼疯了酒店 卫生问题大曝光 2026-11-14 00:02:22 精彩推荐 凌晨3点醒来 是该看S16决赛了 BLG血战GEN 2026-11-13 16:28:31 加载更多

content: 18岁少女检出18种HPV亚型阳性,包含10种高危型;医生发声 北京时间 2026-11-12 23:29发布于北京北京广播电视台《北京时间》官方账号 问AI · 公共场合间接接触是否为青少年感染HPV隐患? 近日,潮新闻·钱报健康小站、杭州市临平区妇幼保健院妇科接诊了一例极其少见的HPV多重感染病例:年仅18岁的玲玲因外阴持续性疼痛半月余前来就诊,最终确诊为外阴尖锐湿疣,且一次性检出18种HPV亚型阳性,其中高危型多达10种,属于临床极少见的多重混合感染。 玲玲的HPV检验报告/医院供图 接诊医生介绍,玲玲来杭探亲,半个月来外阴隐隐疼痛,总觉得有异物感,最近难受得越来越厉害,正常生活都受影响。专科查体发现其外阴长了典型的菜花状赘生物,从外观来看很像尖锐湿疣。为了查清到底感染了哪些病毒,医生给她做了高精度HPV分型检测,结果让人意外:一共查出18种HPV亚型同时阳性,感染的亚型多、病毒载量很高。 HPV分型检测/医院供图 值得高度警惕的是,在18种阳性亚型中,包含10种高危致癌型HPV,是诱发宫颈上皮内病变甚至进展为宫颈癌的核心风险亚型。一次性多重混合感染18种亚型且高危占比极高,提示患者病毒暴露时间长、感染复杂、远期癌变风险显著升高。接诊医生结合玲玲的症状、专科体征及精准HPV分型结果,最终确诊为外阴尖锐湿疣、HPV多重高危感染,目前正在积极治疗中。 新闻多一点 HPV,又叫人乳头瘤病毒。很多人可能以为它只能通过性传播,但实际上一些间接的皮肤接触也很容易感染到HPV。 当我们运动时,皮肤因摩擦会产生肉眼难见的微小破损,后背、手臂直接接触垫面,病毒就会“乘虚而入”。出汗后皮肤角质层软化,屏障减弱,感染风险也会更高。如果抓挠,HPV病毒还会沿抓痕扩散。 不仅如此,HPV病毒还特别喜欢潮湿环境,像是公共的泳池、浴室、浴桶、浴室地垫等也都可能变成“病毒中转站”,共用时特别容易中招。 平时除了要保持良好的个人卫生习惯,做好手部清洁,不与他人共用毛巾、浴盆、内衣裤等私人物品,如果皮肤有伤口,尽量不要去公共场所(如泳池、浴室)。 HPV家族庞大 低危型爱长疣,高危型有肿块 不过幸运的是,HPV是个大家庭,里面有一两百种基因型,不是所有的HPV感染都会发生癌症。 1、低危型HPV感染:皮肤或生殖器长疣 低危型HPV本身没有致癌基因,它引起的多是良性的疣体增生,癌变风险较低。 它一般出现在眼睛周围、手背、前臂等部位,有米粒至黄豆大小,扁平微微鼓起的小丘疹,数目较多且密集,颜色起初呈肉或粉色,时间久了,还会变成深褐色,会有瘙痒感。 除此之外,还有以下4种情况,也都属于低危型HPV感染: 丝状疣:长在额头、脖子上像“小钉子”一样的小肉揪; 寻常疣:手指、手背、指甲周围出现的圆形或不规则硬疙瘩; 跖疣:脚底板上长了硬硬的、走路疼的疙瘩; 尖锐湿疣:HPV病毒6型、11型引起,在私处或肛周出现乳头状、菜花状、鸡冠状的小肉团,可能伴有瘙痒、异物感。 需要特别注意的是尖锐湿疣,它虽然是良性的,但如果长期放任不管、疣体反复破溃发炎,发展成巨大型尖锐湿疣之后,癌变的风险会明显升高,一旦发现请立即就医。 2、高危型HPV:早期无声息,后期有肿块 典型代表就是HPV16型、18型! 致癌性最强,有约70%的宫颈癌是由这两种HPV病毒引起的,还可能引发外阴癌、肛门癌、口咽癌等多种癌症,还有HPV31型、33型、45型、52型、58型等14种,致癌风险都很高。 不过,它们早期通常无症状,到后期才可能出现异常阴道出血、白带异常、局部肿块、小腹坠胀等症状。 3、定期筛查+接种疫苗有助降低HPV风险 所以,定期筛查格外重要,建议大家可以去医院做HPV检测,至少五年一次,还可以做TCT(宫颈脱落细胞学)检查,至少三年一次。 尤其是在感染HPV的高峰年龄段(女性20岁、45岁,男性20岁、60岁),性行为过早、雌激素波动,还有抵抗力下降等因素都会让HPV病毒更易入侵,尤其女性,一生有80%的几率会感染HPV。 平时除了要保持良好的个人卫生习惯,做好手部清洁,不与他人共用毛巾、浴盆、内衣裤等私人物品,在公共场所(如泳池、浴室),避免通过微小皮肤破损间接感染。 此外,还可以选择接种疫苗,来帮助预防感染HPV病毒。 比如说现在的九价疫苗,它不仅能预防16型、18型、31型、33型、45型、52型、58型等7种HPV高危病毒感染。 还能额外预防引发尖锐湿疣的HPV低危型病毒(6型、11型),满足日常防护需求,9-45岁的女性,9-26岁的男性都可以去接种。 总结一下 1、间接的皮肤接触也可能导致HPV感染; 2、HPV高危型病毒早期无症状,到后期才会出现阴道出血、小腹坠胀、白带异常等表现,建议尽早接种疫苗,定期做好HPV检测和TCT检查。 来源:北京时间综合 潮新闻、海峡导报、北京卫视我是大医生官微 文章推荐

接诊医生介绍,年仅18岁的玲玲,半个月来外阴隐隐疼痛,总觉得有异物感,最近难受得越来越厉害,正常生活都受影响。专科查体发现其外阴长了典型的菜花状赘生物,从外观来看很像尖锐湿疣。 为了查清到底感染了哪些病毒,医生给她做了高精度HPV分型检测,结果让人意外:一共查出18种HPV亚型同时阳性,感染的亚型多、病毒载量很高,属于临床极少见的多重混合感染。 玲玲的HPV检验报告。 值得高度警惕的是,在18种阳性亚型中,包含10种高危致癌型HPV,是诱发宫颈上皮内病变,甚至进展为宫颈癌的核心风险亚型。 一次性多重混合感染18种亚型且高危占比极高,提示患者病毒暴露时间长、感染复杂、远期癌变风险显著升高。 科普时间: HPV分为高危型和低危型, 绝大多数感染是一过性的, 但若有这一情况,可能导致癌变 HPV(人乳头瘤病毒)是一种专门感染人类皮肤和黏膜的DNA病毒。主要通过性接触传播,也可通过皮肤或黏膜的直接接触传播。很多人一生中至少会感染一次,属于人群感染率很高的疾病之一。 HPV家族非常庞大,目前已发现的亚型超过200种,整体分为高危型和低危型↓↓ ■高危型HPV:主要与恶性肿瘤相关,持续感染可能引发宫颈癌、肛门癌、阴道癌、阴茎癌、口腔癌等。常见亚型包括HPV16、18、31、33、45、52、58等,其中HPV16和18型是导致全球约70%宫颈癌的主要元凶。只要查出16型或18型阳性,建议进一步做阴道镜检查。 ■ 低危型HPV:更容易感染手、足等部位的皮肤,会引起寻常疣、跖疣。这些皮肤型HPV并不需要通过性接触传播,可以通过皮肤直接接触传播,如被污染的毛巾、鞋袜、公共淋浴间地面和泳池边地面传播。一般不会导致宫颈癌。 而尖锐湿疣,医学上称为生殖器疣,6型和11型是导致尖锐湿疣的“罪魁祸首”,约90%的病例由它们引起。尖锐湿疣典型的特征是呈菜花样,可伴随疼痛、异物感。 绝大多数感染都是一过性的。人体自身免疫力,通常可以在1至2年内把病毒清除掉,并不会发展成病变。 只有同一高危型HPV持续感染,才可能进展为癌前病变,再进一步变成癌,当中往往需要数年甚至十几年时间。 医生提醒: 尽量避免共用毛巾、拖鞋等物品, 建议接种HPV疫苗,做好定期筛查 医生提醒,阻断HPV,平时生活中做好预防—— ■ 不抽烟、少喝酒、少熬夜、多锻炼身体,提高自身免疫力。 ■ 尽量避免共用私人物品,如毛巾、拖鞋、指甲刀等,并做好定期清洗消毒。 ■ 接种HPV疫苗,主动预防感染。 ■ 定期宫颈筛查。一般女性从25至30岁开始,从公共卫生角度,每3至5年做一次HPV检测;从临床角度,每2年做一次筛查可能更为稳妥。 ■ 若不幸确诊,遵医嘱规范治疗,发现得越早,治疗效果越好。 According to the investigation conducted by researchers at King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Centre, Alfaisal University, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University, and Jazan University, persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) remains necessary but insufficient on its own to cause cervical cancer. The synthesis evaluated whether common sexually transmitted co-infections—specifically Chlamydia trachomatis, herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), and HIV—serve as independent biological co-factors that drive malignant transformation. The global health burden underlying the investigation is substantial, as cervical cancer was responsible for approximately 350,000 deaths in 2022 alone. While the oncogenic activity of persistent HR-HPV is well established, secondary modifiers have long been proposed to accelerate or enable neoplastic progression. However, determining true causal inference across existing studies has been challenged by pervasive residual confounding, extensive methodological heterogeneity between published investigations, and a notable lack of mechanistic validation conducted directly in human cervical tissue. Discover more infections Infections Infectious To clarify these relationships, the investigators structured their work as a systematic integrative review adhering to PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The team conducted comprehensive literature searches across five major biomedical databases—PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library—covering research published between January 2015 and March 2026. Methodological quality and risk of bias within observational datasets were evaluated using established tools, specifically the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and the ROBINS-I instrument, while the overall certainty of evidence for each pathogen was appraised using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. Discover more Book a Checkup Check Symptoms See an OB-GYN Find Cancer Care Among the examined pathogens, HIV demonstrated the most consistent and robust epidemiological evidence, receiving a GRADE certainty rating of high. Co-infection with HIV was associated with an approximate six-fold elevation in cervical cancer risk, reinforced by a confirmed CD4 cell count dose-response relationship. Furthermore, the review noted that a residual risk persists even among women receiving antiretroviral therapy, reflecting a three- to four-fold risk elevation in virologically suppressed populations. These epidemiological patterns establish HIV as meeting the criteria for a probable causal modifier in HPV-induced cervical malignancy, directly supporting World Health Organization guidelines that endorse intensified screening programs for women living with HIV. In contrast, the evidence implicating Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) remains far less definitive, receiving a GRADE certainty rating of low to moderate. While initial observational studies have linked CT co-infection to two- to four-fold increases in cervical neoplasia, the pooled association is compromised by significant heterogeneity across study designs and lingering confounding related to sexual behavior. Funnel-plot asymmetry across the identified publications also suggests the presence of publication bias. Most notably, when models were adjusted for baseline HPV status, the independent effect of CT attenuated substantially to an odds ratio of 1.76, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 1.03 to 3.01, leaving its status as an independent causal driver unproven. The findings regarding herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) were similarly equivocal, resulting in a GRADE rating of low certainty. Although unadjusted pooled estimates indicated an elevated cervical cancer risk with an odds ratio of 3.01 (95% confidence interval 2.24 to 4.04), the vast majority of analyzed studies failed to control for underlying HPV infection status. When prospective cohorts were examined specifically, the observed associations failed to reach statistical significance. Additionally, available mechanistic support for HSV-2 activity is currently limited to non-human biological models rather than validated human cellular assays, preventing HSV-2 from meeting the established scientific threshold for classification as an independent oncogenic co-factor, despite evidence of a context-dependent syndemic effect observed in populations co-infected with HIV. Based on these findings, the authors concluded that public health and clinical paradigms must distinguish established causal modifiers from unconfirmed co-infections. While intensified cervical cancer screening remains firmly justified for women living with HIV, clarifying the prospective roles of Chlamydia trachomatis and HSV-2 will require rigorous adjustment for sexual behavior and HPV exposure. Moving forward, the review emphasizes that future research priorities must center on well-designed prospective longitudinal cohorts and definitive mechanistic validation performed directly within human cervical tissue. 卫生署卫生防护中心(中心)十一月十二日提醒市民,政府于二○二四年推出的一次性人类乳头瘤病毒(HPV)疫苗补种计划(补种计划)将于今年十二月三十一日结束。已在补种计划下接种第一剂疫苗*的合资格女性香港居民,应把握时间完成余下的接种程序,以免错过免费接种的最后机会。 接种HPV疫苗可有效预防可致命的子宫颈癌。补种计划推出将近两年,累计接种超过74 000剂疫苗。已在补种计划下接种第一剂疫苗*的合资格女性香港居民请尽快联络乐妍站或指定地区康健中心/站,完成余下的接种,否则日后需要自行安排和自费接种。 补种计划下,在二○○四年至二○○八年出生而未完成接种HPV疫苗的合资格女性香港居民可免费接种两剂疫苗,免疫力弱的人士则需接种三剂(三剂均为免费)。免疫功能正常的女性接种两剂HPV疫苗的建议时间为至少相隔五个月。合资格女性香港居民只需先登记“医健通”,即可透过网页或电话(2855 1333)安排到医务卫生局基层医疗署辖下的乐妍站或指定地区康健中心/站接种HPV疫苗(详情请参阅附件)。 补种计划得以顺利推展,中心衷心感谢各中学、专上院校的鼎力支持。中心一直积极宣传补种计划,包括在专上院校设立资讯站、安排卫生署外展队前往护士培训学院、纪律部队训练学校、制服团队及相关机构等安排补种。 个别市民对HPV疫苗存有一定的误解,例如误以为性生活紊乱、拥有多个性伴侣的人士才会感染HPV,或担心接种疫苗会有副作用等。事实上,HPV疫苗已在全球使用多年,世界卫生组织(世卫)和海外卫生部门已表明HPV疫苗安全有效。研究亦表明,接种HPV疫苗不会让孩子性活跃或提早发生性行为。中心呼吁合资格女性香港居民把握最后机会,在十二月三十一日前透过补种计划完成免费的HPV疫苗接种,为自己的健康出一分力,减低感染子宫颈癌的机会。 子宫颈癌于本港女性致命癌症中排第九位,于二○二四年有160名女性死于此癌症。几乎所有子宫颈癌均由持续感染高风险类型的HPV所引致。HPV疫苗能有效预防高风险HPV,包括HPV 16型和18型,其保护力高逾九成。世卫建议所有国家引入HPV疫苗,为九至14岁的女孩在未开始有性接触前接种,并建议对九至18岁(包括先前错过接种的女孩和年龄较大的女孩)进行补种,以减低他们患上子宫颈癌的机会。
